entry.title: Develop, deploy and validate AI-native applications.
entry.body: Platform Loops (PL) is for developers, architects, product managers, business analysts and business users. Describe what you want to improve; PL discovers and proposes the application, carries it through design, build and verification, and releases it into EAL where your users work. Ask the guide anything below. Every answer ends with the next questions worth asking, and every question can also be typed into your PL chat.

topics.title: PL turns business needs into governed, working applications
topics.prompt: What is this platform, and what problem is it designed to solve?
topics.summary: Platform Loops (PL) is a governed development loop: you describe a business need, PL discovers what to build, proposes and designs it, builds and verifies it, and releases it into a runtime where your users work.
takeaways: One conversation carries a need from words to a running, verified application.
Every step leaves evidence: decisions, hashes, tests, browser checks, releases.
PL proposes and executes; you decide at typed gates; nothing external happens without authority.

blocks.text: Platform Loops (PL LOOP) is the development loop of the Intelligent Platform. It exists to close the gap between a business need and a working, trustworthy application without a long specification, a hand-off to a development team, or a black box that produces code nobody can verify. You start with a problem in plain words; PL discovers the actors, process, data and rules, proposes the application, writes the design and plan, generates and verifies the code, and releases it to the Enterprise AI Launchpad (EAL) where people use it.

blocks.caption: The loop in one picture: every arm is a question you can ask next.

blocks.text: The problems it is designed to solve

rows.label: Lost intent
rows.value: Requirements written once and forgotten. PL keeps a living record of what was understood, decided, assumed and still open.

rows.label: Slow hand-offs
rows.value: Analysis, design, build and test done by different people in sequence. PL carries one thread from idea to release with you approving at typed gates.

rows.label: Unverifiable code
rows.value: Generated code you cannot trust. PL traces every requirement to tests and browser evidence and records hashes for every file.

rows.label: Uncontrolled AI
rows.value: Agents that act on their own. PL never builds, deploys or touches external systems without an explicit approval from you.

blocks.title: What PL is not
blocks.text: PL is not a chatbot that writes code snippets, and not a no-code form designer. It is a control plane that runs a governed loop and keeps evidence for every step.

blocks.text: PL is primarily used to deliver business applications: worklists, forms, approval flows, calendars, case timelines and analytical lists that run on a UI, an API and a PostgreSQL database with proper roles. Its second use is evolving those applications safely once they exist. Its third use is answering questions and giving coding help in the same chat, without changing anything.

blocks.text: The sweet spot today is a single-entity business application with two or three roles, delivered in under an hour. Larger scopes are delivered as several bounded applications.

topics.title: Start with one problem in plain words; PL leads from there
topics.prompt: I am new to this platform. How should I get started?
topics.summary: Create a project, describe one problem in a few sentences, accept the recommended defaults one at a time, approve the Blueprint, confirm Local defaults, and let PL take you through requirements to a running app.
takeaways: Describe the problem, not the solution; three to six sentences are enough.
Accept defaults one card at a time and approve the Blueprint before anything else.
Follow the next-step chip; it always carries the right command for the active revision.

blocks.caption: A first project takes about 30 to 45 minutes of your attention; PL does the rest.

steps.label: Answer one question at a time

items.title: Create a project
items.detail: Use the Projects panel on the left. Name it after the application, for example Mileage Reimbursement Log. A project holds one application and its chats.

items.title: Describe the problem, not the solution
items.detail: Who struggles, how the work happens now, what should improve, which fields and rules matter. Add: Scope: Local Development only. Finish with: Finalize discovery from this description and generate the Discovery Blueprint for review. Do not design or build yet.

items.title: Accept defaults one card at a time
items.detail: PL proposes measurable defaults (rounding rule, who sees what). Click the recommended option or answer in your own words. Do not ask PL to apply all defaults at once; it answers within a per-turn model-call limit.

items.title: Approve the Discovery Blueprint
items.detail: Read it as the whole understanding in one card. Corrections are cheap here and expensive later.

items.title: Confirm where it runs
items.detail: Accept the nudge Use Local defaults and confirm. It places the UI, API and database schema on your workstation.

items.title: Follow the next-step chip
items.detail: The composer offers the next lifecycle command: Requirements, then Delivery Plan, Solution Design and Build Plan. Approve each; request changes in Requirements, not later.

items.title: Start build and accept
items.detail: Send Start build. Watch the steps, review the Business Review evidence, accept the release, and open the app in EAL with the test identity PL created.

blocks.title: Two phrases to avoid
blocks.text: Never write I confirm the topology or I confirm the architecture; the evaluator treats that as an authority conflict and the discovery loops. Confirm business facts only, as the requesting user. And never ask PL to apply defaults without asking.

plPrompts.prompt: Help me turn a business problem into an application idea. Start with three simple examples, propose a direction, and ask one question at a time. Do not build anything.

topics.prompt: What are the main components of this platform, and what is the purpose of each component?
topics.summary: PL (development loop) and EAL (runtime loop) are the two general-purpose loops; UME, EKG with Platform Brain, the Integration plane, Audit, Eval Studio and the Control Center are the services around them, plus the applications PL generates.

blocks.caption: Every service owns its own database; nothing reads another service's tables.

Identity: principals, roles, sessions, effective access; publishes app roles
Enterprise Knowledge Graph and organisational knowledge: landscape, lineage, questions about apps
Governed connectors (PostgreSQL, files) for integration-backed apps
Apps that read or write a system of record

topics.title: During delivery the components hand work to each other in a fixed order
topics.prompt: How do the different platform components work together during application development?
topics.summary: PL owns the loop; EKG answers landscape questions; the builder generates the app; delivery provisions the database, registers the release with EAL and publishes roles to UME; EAL launches the app for users; Audit and Eval Studio observe.

blocks.caption: Hand-offs during one delivery. Audit and Eval Studio observe every lane.

items: PL understands your message, routes it to a capability, and keeps the session and delivery case as an event log.
When you confirm where the app runs, PL asks the landscape provider (EKG, or Local defaults when EKG is offline) for placement.
The builder turns the approved Build Plan into source files: UI, API, domain, migrations, tests.
Delivery provisions a PostgreSQL schema with the app's own login, runs migrations, builds and starts the API and UI on reserved ports, and verifies them.
Delivery registers a signed release set with the EAL registry and publishes the app's roles to UME; a test identity is created for you.
Business Review shows browser evidence; when you accept, the release is activated in EAL and users can open it.
Every step writes receipts: artifact manifests with hashes, delivery journal, audit envelopes; Eval Studio can replay and score the run.

blocks.text: Nothing crosses a boundary by reading another service's database. Components talk over signed HTTP contracts, which is why a release can be rolled back and why evidence is attributable.

topics.title: From your idea to a running application and its improvement
topics.prompt: Finally, explain how the entire platform works together, from a user's initial idea to a running production application and its continuous improvement.
topics.summary: One thread: understand, shape, design and plan, build and verify, release and run, observe and improve. PL owns the thread, EAL runs the result, the services around them keep identity, knowledge, evidence and operations honest.
takeaways: One canonical record connects messages, decisions, work products, files, releases and usage.
PL is the development loop, EAL the runtime loop; UME, EKG, Audit and Eval keep them honest.
Today everything runs in Local Development; QA, UAT and Production are planned, not available.

blocks.caption: The same thread continues for every later version of the application.

items.label: Understand
items.detail: You describe the need; PL discovers actors, process, data and rules and proposes the Discovery Blueprint.

items.label: Shape
items.detail: You approve the Blueprint and confirm where it runs; PL writes Requirements and the Delivery Plan.

items.label: Design and plan
items.detail: Solution Design and Build Plan, each reviewed as consequence and diff.

items.label: Build and verify
items.detail: Generated UI, API, database and tests; typecheck, tests, browser qualification; hashes and receipts.

items.label: Release and run
items.detail: Business Review, activation in EAL, roles in UME; users sign in and work.

items.label: Observe and improve
items.detail: Runtime observations, evaluations and your change requests feed the next version through impact analysis.

blocks.text: The platform works because one canonical record connects everything. Your messages become events; events become decisions and work products; work products become generated files with hashes; files become a release with a manifest; the release becomes a registered application in EAL with roles from UME; use in EAL produces observations; observations and your new requests start the next revision, which traces back to the same Blueprint. Knowledge about the application lives in the project ledger and, when enabled, in the Platform Brain and the Enterprise Knowledge Graph, so the platform can answer questions about the application months later.

blocks.title: Honest scope today
blocks.text: Applications run in Local Development on the platform workstation. Central Development, QA, UAT and Production environments are designed and sequenced in the roadmap but are not yet available. Everything else in this answer is what the platform does now.

topics.title: For developers, architects, product managers, business analysts and business users
topics.prompt: Who is this platform for?
topics.summary: Anyone who owns a business need can develop, deploy and validate an AI-native application with PL. Business users and analysts drive discovery and acceptance, product managers scope and approve, architects and developers review design and build plans, and everyone validates the result in EAL.
takeaways: One chat serves every role; nobody needs to write code or a specification first.
Business roles own intent and acceptance; technical roles own design review and evolution.
AI-native means the application is generated, verified and run by the platform with roles, audit and a conversational runtime built in.

blocks.caption: Every role works in the same PL chat and validates in the same EAL runtime.
Develop, deploy, validate. Click a step for what each role does.

steps.label: Develop
steps.detail: Describe the need in the PL chat; PL discovers, proposes the Blueprint, writes requirements, design and build plan, and generates the application with tests. Business and technical roles approve at typed gates.

steps.label: Deploy
steps.detail: PL provisions the database schema and login, builds and starts the UI and API on reserved ports, registers the signed release with EAL and publishes roles to UME. Today this is Local Development; later environments are promoted by release manifest.

steps.label: Validate
steps.detail: Business Review shows browser evidence against requirements; you accept or reject. Then every role signs in to EAL with their own role and uses the application: chat, forms, approvals, full view.

Read the Business Review evidence; add acceptance signals

blocks.title: What AI-native means here
blocks.text: The application is produced from a typed Blueprint by the platform, carries its roles, audit and idempotency by construction, is used through a conversational runtime as well as a full UI, and is evolved through the same governed loop that created it.

topics.title: EAL: the runtime where AI-native applications are used
topics.prompt: What is EAL and what is it used for?
topics.summary: EAL, the Enterprise AI Launchpad, is the runtime loop of the platform. Users sign in, find their applications, chat with registered tasks, fill confirmed forms, approve human tasks and open the full UI. PL builds and releases; EAL runs. Roles come from UME; every write is confirmed and receipted.
takeaways: EAL is where business users live; PL is where applications are made.
Everything a user can do in EAL is a registered task or form published by the application's release.
Writes are confirmed by the user and receipted by the application; nothing happens silently.

blocks.text: What EAL is used for

rows: Signs in once; sees the applications assigned to their roles
UME resolves principals, roles and effective access
Types a registered task phrase, for example Create a mileage log record.
Deterministic routing to the registered task; the app API is called with signed authority
Completes the registered form, reviews, confirms
Field values are synchronised; the API validates and writes with an idempotency receipt
Claims, approves, rejects, delegates human tasks
Human-workflow state machine with role checks; password step-up for sensitive actions
Launches the generated UI (worklist, form, timeline)
EAL passes a signed authority reference; the API resolves it live
Previews assignments, sets retention and legal holds, exports privacy data

topics.title: The application development process, as a process diagram
topics.prompt: Show me the app development process as a process diagram.
topics.summary: Eight steps from a business problem to a running application. Four of them are your decisions; the rest are automated and evidenced by PL. Click any step for what happens, who decides and what it produces.
takeaways: Your decisions: approve the Blueprint, approve the work products, authorize Start build, accept the Business Review.
Everything between your decisions is automated and leaves evidence: manifests, tests, browser checks.
The same eight steps repeat for every later version of the application.

blocks.caption: The development process.

steps.label: Describe
steps.detail: Type the problem in plain words: who struggles, how the work happens today, what should improve, the fields and rules that matter. End with the request to generate the Discovery Blueprint. Three to eight sentences are enough.

steps.label: Discover
steps.detail: PL extracts the outcome, actors, journeys, data, rules and risks, then asks one question per turn with a measurable default you can accept or correct. It stops when enough dimensions are covered.

steps.label: Blueprint
steps.detail: The whole understanding in one card: entity, fields, states, roles, screens and a topology recommendation. Approve it or request a change. This is the cheapest moment to fix a misunderstanding.

steps.label: Requirements
steps.detail: Testable statements with validation rules and acceptance signals, each traced to the Blueprint. Approving starts the chain of downstream work products; later changes here cascade.

steps.label: Design and plan
steps.detail: Delivery Plan (which stages apply), Solution Design (components, contracts, data ownership) and Build Plan (exact files, migrations, tests). Each shown as what it decides plus a diff.
steps.artifact: Delivery Plan, Solution Design, Build Plan

steps.label: Build and verify
steps.detail: Scaffold, generate, provision the schema and login, migrate, build, start on reserved ports, typecheck, tests and browser qualification. PL only interrupts if it needs you.

steps.label: Review and release
steps.detail: The Business Review lists requirement-derived checks with evidence observed in a real browser. Accept to activate the release in EAL and publish roles to UME.

steps.label: Run and improve
steps.detail: Users sign in to EAL and work in chat or the full view. Change requests come back into the same project with impact analysis and a new version.

rows.label: Who decides
rows.value: Blueprint, Requirements and downstream approvals, Start build, and the Business Review are yours. Nothing passes those points without a typed decision.

rows.label: What is automated
rows.value: Understanding, discovery questions, drafting of every work product, generation, provisioning, building, testing, browser qualification, packaging, registration and role publication.

rows.label: What is recorded
rows.value: Every message, decision and result as events; every file with a SHA-256; every build with receipts; every release with an identity.

plPrompts.prompt: Show me the app development process on this platform as an ordered list of steps, marking which steps need my decision and what each step produces. Do not start execution.

topics.title: Cross-functional delivery: who does what, in order
topics.prompt: Show the app delivery process as a cross-functional swimlane diagram.
topics.summary: Four lanes and thirteen steps. Business decides, architects and developers review, PL discovers, drafts, generates and verifies, and the runtime registers and serves the application. Click any box for the details of that step.
takeaways: Hand-offs alternate between a human decision and platform work; no lane skips another.
PL never enters the business lane: it proposes, you decide.
The runtime lane starts only after your acceptance in the Business Review.

blocks.caption: Cross-functional delivery.

sequence.label: Describe the need
sequence.detail: Create a project and describe the problem in plain words: people, current situation, desired improvement, fields, rules and examples. End with the request to generate the Discovery Blueprint.

sequence.label: Discover
sequence.detail: PL extracts actors, journeys, data, rules and risks and asks one question per turn with a measurable default. Option cards wait for the business answer; the composer is paused meanwhile.

sequence.label: Approve Blueprint
sequence.detail: Review the entity, fields, states, roles, screens and topology recommendation in one card. Approve, or request a change and approve the next version.

sequence.label: Confirm landscape
sequence.detail: Decide where the application runs. Local defaults place the UI, API and PostgreSQL schema on the platform host in one click; EKG can propose placements when it is online.

sequence.label: Requirements
sequence.detail: Testable statements, validation rules and acceptance signals, each traced to a Blueprint item.

sequence.label: Approve Requirements
sequence.detail: Approving starts the downstream chain. A later change to Requirements supersedes the Delivery Plan, Solution Design and Build Plan, which regenerate in order.

sequence.label: Plan, design, build plan
sequence.detail: Delivery Plan: which stages apply and the verification each needs. Solution Design: components, contracts, data ownership. Build Plan: exact files, migrations and tests.

sequence.label: Review design and plan
sequence.detail: The architect reviews components and data ownership; the developer reviews files and tests. Precise change requests go into Requirements so the cascade carries them.

sequence.label: Start build.
sequence.detail: Authorizes generation and local execution. Eligible only when all four work products are approved on the active revision and the session budget allows it.

sequence.label: Generate, provision, verify
sequence.detail: Scaffold, generate source, create the schema and a NOBYPASSRLS login, migrate, build, start on reserved ports, run typecheck, tests and browser qualification, record the release identity.

sequence.label: Register release, publish roles
sequence.detail: A signed release set is staged in the EAL registry; the application's roles are published to UME; a test identity is created for validation.

sequence.label: Accept in Business Review
sequence.detail: Read requirement-derived checks with browser evidence. Accept to activate; reject with a reason to return to Requirements.

sequence.label: Users work in EAL
sequence.detail: Users sign in with their roles, chat with registered tasks, fill confirmed forms, approve human tasks and open the full view. Every write is receipted and audited.

rows: Solution Design and Build Plan drafted

blocks.text: For an evolution of a released application the same lanes apply from Requirements onward, with an impact analysis step in the PL lane before regeneration.

plPrompts.prompt: Show the app delivery process on this platform as a cross-functional view: for each step, who acts (business user, architect or developer, the platform, the runtime) and what is handed over. Do not start execution.

topics.title: The application lifecycle: create or migrate, release, operate, enhance, release again
topics.prompt: What is the application lifecycle?
topics.summary: An AI-native application is created new or migrated from a legacy application, released through DEV, QA and PRD, operated, enhanced and released again. Today PL delivers the create-and-enhance loop in Local Development (DEV) and runs the app in EAL; QA and PRD promotion and legacy migration are designed and sequenced on the roadmap.
takeaways: Two entry paths: a new AI-native application, or a legacy application migrated into one.
Two ongoing loops: enhance and release again; migrate an AI-native application between environments by promoting its immutable release.
Available today: create, enhance, release to DEV, run in EAL. Planned: QA and PRD promotion, legacy migration.
topics.statusNote: DEV today; QA and PRD promotion planned

blocks.caption: Create or migrate, then release. Click a step for details and status.

steps.label: New idea or legacy app
steps.detail: A new AI-native application starts from a problem statement. A legacy application enters through modernization: repository and runtime discovery, a characterization baseline that is green before any change, and strangler increments. Modernization is planned; new applications are available today.

steps.label: Develop with PL
steps.detail: Discovery, Blueprint, Requirements, Delivery Plan, Solution Design, Build Plan, build and verification through the governed loop.

steps.label: Release to DEV
steps.detail: Local Development: schema and login provisioned, UI and API started on reserved ports, signed release registered in EAL, roles published to UME, Business Review accepted.

steps.label: Promote to QA
steps.detail: The immutable release manifest is promoted to a QA environment with its evidence; qualification runs there without rebuilding. Planned with the environment ladder.

steps.label: Promote to PRD
steps.detail: Production promotion under a customer-controlled installation with identity federation, secret references, backup and recovery drills. Planned with the deployment foundation.

steps.label: Operate
steps.detail: Users work in EAL; the Control Center monitors platform services; audit and activity are recorded; observations feed the next change.

blocks.caption: Enhance and release again; migrate between environments by promotion.

steps.label: Enhance
steps.detail: Describe the change in the application's project. PL classifies it as an evolution, shows the impact (fields, screens, rules, tests) and asks for approval.

steps.label: Regenerate
steps.detail: Downstream work products regenerate in order from canonical inputs; unchanged parts are byte-identical; migrations are additive and prior bytes preserved.
steps.artifact: Design and plan v2, new migration

steps.label: Verify
steps.detail: Existing tests must pass; new tests cover the change; browser qualification repeats the business checks.

steps.label: Release to DEV
steps.detail: A new release directory and identity; activation replaces the previous release in EAL; the previous one is kept for rollback.

steps.label: Promote QA, PRD
steps.detail: Migrating an AI-native application between environments means promoting the same immutable release through the environment gates, never rebuilding it.

topics.prompt: How does the platform determine which development activities can be automated and which ones require human approval?
topics.summary: PL automates analysis, drafting, generation, verification and packaging. topics.title: Traceability, deterministic generation and evidence keep applications correct
topics.prompt: How does the platform ensure that generated applications meet requirements and are technically correct?
topics.summary: Requirements trace to acceptance criteria and tests; generation is deterministic from the approved Blueprint; every build runs typecheck, tests and a browser qualification with independently supplied expected values; hashes and receipts make the result reviewable.

blocks.caption: The traceability engine assembles this matrix; the Business Review shows it.

rows.label: Meets requirements
rows.value: A traceability matrix links requirements to criteria and tests; browser qualification drives the running app with a business oracle whose expected values come from outside the model.

rows.label: Technically correct
rows.value: Deterministic generators produce typed domain, API and UI code; typecheck, unit and contract tests, build and start must pass; ports, schema and identity are verified after deployment, not assumed.

rows.label: Secure by construction
rows.value: Generated APIs enforce per-action authorization and idempotency receipts; the app runs with its own database login; EAL authority is resolved live for every request.

rows.label: Reviewable
rows.value: Artifact manifests with SHA-256 per file, immutable release directories, provenance gate on commits, delivery journal with every receipt.

blocks.text: Correctness is proven for what was specified. If a rule is missing from Requirements, no test will catch it; that is why the guide keeps sending you back to Requirements for changes.

blocks.text: Applications are single-entity per generation; multi-entity domains are delivered as several apps. topics.title: Procedure: approving, requesting changes and the cascade
topics.prompt: How do approvals and Request change work?
topics.summary: Each work product card has Approve and Request change. Approving records a typed decision; Request change stores a rejection and asks for the correction; content is fixed by regenerating the earliest affected work product, usually Requirements.

rows.label: Approve
rows.value: Records your decision on this version; the next-step chip advances.

rows.label: Request change
